question.text: The Ottomans conquered this capital city of the Byzantine Empire in May 1453. Give its name as of 1453, not its ancient name or its modern name, which was adopted in 1923.
question.answerHtml: Constantinople (do not accept or prompt on “Byzantium” or “Istanbul”)
question.clue: Enrico Dandolo redirected the Fourth Crusade to attack this city, the location where Belisarius slaughtered a mob in the Hippodrome during the Nika Riots.

swap.text: The Byzantine Empire had several rulers with this common name; the first of whom usurped the throne from Michael III and founded the Macedonian dynasty, and the second was known as the Bulgar-slayer for his complete conquest of Bulgaria.
swap.clue: The Varangian Guard was expanded after a ruler of this name married his sister Anna to Vladimir I ("the first") of Kiev.

question.leadin: His financial advisor was Peter Barsymes.
question.text: Name this Byzantine Emperor who hired Anthemios of Tralles and Izidorus of Miletus to design the Hagia Sophia. He also established a namesake code.
question.clue: This ruler was alleged to be a demon by the "Secret History" of his follower Procopius.

swap.leadin: His generals included Belisarius and Narses, and the Nika Riots threatened to unseat him.
swap.text: Name this Byzantine emperor, the husband of Theodora, who was responsible for the Corpus Iuris Civilis.
swap.answerHtml: Justinian the Great [accept Justinian I, or Flavius Petrus Sabbatius Justinianus, prompt on Justinian]
swap.clue: The scholar Tribonian headed a commission that published namesake "novels" that solved contradictions within a law code named for this ruler.

question.leadin: This Byzantine general's last victory came in 559 A.D. when he defeated a force of Huns and Slavs outside of Constantinople.
question.text: Name this general who conquered the Vandal kingdom in Africa at the Battle of Tricameron and who went on to fight and conquer most of the Ostrogothic kingdom of Italy.
question.clue: This general's campaigns informed Procopius's History of the Wars.

swap.text: Constantinople was earlier sacked during this campaign, which led to the decline of the Byzantine Empire. Enrico Dandolo, the Doge of Venice, had earlier led this campaign.
swap.clue: In order to obtain the support of one city state, the participants of this event agreed to sack the city of Zara in Hungary.

question.text: This Byzantine emperor defeated the Sassanids at the 627 Battle of Nineveh. Unfortunately for this emperor's reputation, the resulting peace was ended when the Muslims conquered all of Mesopotamia and North Africa.
question.clue: Jacobus de Voragine's hagiography The Golden Legend documents this ruler's recovery of a piece of the True Cross.

swap.text: This liquid weapon of the Byzantine empire was invented during the reign of Emperor Constantine IV by a Greek-speaking Syrian refugee. It was thrown onto enemy ships and burst into flames on contact.
swap.clue: Leo VI supposedly invented a handheld version of this weapon called a cheirosiphones, which was later thought to be particularly effective against siege towers.

question.text: The Byzantine Empire went through periods characterized by this belief, the opposition to the use of religious images.
question.clue: The first attempt to apply this doctrine officially was met with resistance at the Chalke Gate, and it was condemned by the Second Council of Nicaea convoked by Irene.

swap.leadin: Identify the following about some military units charged with protecting heads of state.
swap.text: Known for bearing axes and being comprised largely of Scandinavians, these troops were the guards of the Byzantine Empire. This unit was established by Basil II.
swap.clue: As punishment for replacing this group with loyal Scythians, Michael V ("the fifth") was castrated and blinded by Harald Hardrada.

question.leadin: Answer the following about the 1453 conquest of Constantinople by the Ottoman Empire.
question.text: The death of Constantine XI during the battle brought an end to the two hundred year rule of this final dynasty of Byzantine emperors.
question.clue: This dynasty's founder wedded his daughter into the noble family of Trebizond; that founder was Michael VIII. Its last ruler, Constantine XI, died in the Ottomans' siege of Constantinople.

swap.leadin: His Corpus Juris Civilis codified Roman law, and his numerous building projects included the Hagia Sofia.
swap.text: Name this husband of Theodora, a Byzantine emperor whose rule was chronicled by Procopius.
swap.answerHtml: Justinian I the Great [or Flavius Petrus Sabbatius or Favius Anicius Justinianus Magnus]

question.text: The Council of Clermont was ostensibly called to assist this embattled Byzantine emperor, who did not ask for a full-scale invasion of the Holy Land. Still, he took advantage of the Crusade to regain lost territory in Anatolia.
question.clue: The insane monk Raiktor joined a force against this man that won the Battle of Dyrrhachium and Robert Guiscard.

swap.text: The most famous member of this family temporarily ended the Great Schism with the Second Council of Lyon after reclaiming Constantinople from the Latin Empire. That man, Michael VIII, established this family as the final Byzantine dynasty.
swap.clue: Michael VIII founded this dynasty, which expelled the Crusaders from Constantinople in 1261 and were the last to rule Byzantium before the Turkish conquest in 1453.

question.text: After the Battle of Adrianople, the Bulgar tsar Kaloyan made a cup from the skull of the first Latin Emperor, who had this name. The final ruler of the Latin Empire, who sold the Crown of Thorns to Louis IX, also had this name.
question.answerHtml: Baldwin [or Baudouin; or Baldwin I; or Baldwin II; or Baldwin of Courtenay]
question.clue: This cousin of Rudyard Kipling highlighted the power of aerial attacks by noting that "the bomber will always get through."

swap.leadin: The Arsenites and Josephists feuded over support for this ruler, whom Patriarch Arsenios Autoreianos had excommunicated in 1261 for ordering the blinding of the eleven-year-old John IV Laskaris.
swap.text: Name this ruler whose policies were juxtaposed with those of his son, Andronikos II, by the contemporaneous historian George Pachymeres ("pack-ih-MEER-eez").
swap.clue: This figure's diplomatic acumen and willingness to bankrupt his treasury helped Pedro III of Aragon, overthrowing Charles of Anjou in the Sicilian Vespers.

question.text: This woman wrote admiringly of the manly traits of Empress Irene in her influential Byzantine history, The Alexiad.
question.clue: This woman may have been inspired by the material laid out by her husband Nikephoros Bryennios the Younger to write a chronicle of her father's rule named the Alexiad.

swap.leadin: This ruler recognized Stefan Nemanja ("NEH-mahn-yah") as the rightful zupan ("zhoo-pan") during an incredibly successful campaign through Serbia.
swap.text: Identify this expansionist Byzantine emperor whose reign was chronicled by his loyal historian John Cinnamus. He magnanimously forgave Raynald of Chatillon ("shah-tee-YON") for his Cyprian massacre in exchange for total fealty.
swap.clue: While this ruler's armies besieged the island of Corfu, the Venetians mocked this ruler by having an African slave impersonate him.

question.text: A Pecheneg siege of Constantinople in 1090 was defeated by this Byzantine emperor and his Cuman allies. His daughter Anna Comnenus wrote a biography of him, and he ruled during the First Crusade.
question.clue: This ruler lost the Battle of Dyrrhachium to Robert Guiscard during a Norman invasion of his territory; Guiscard's death is related in Book 6 of a historical text compiled by this man's daughter, Anna, and named for him.

swap.leadin: Answer the following about the invasion of Byzantine Greece by Murad II.
swap.text: At that time, the entire Peloponnese was under the control of this Despotate, which had been established circa 1349 by Byzantine emperor John VI Cantacuzenus, and then taken over by the Palaeologus dynasty. It was ruled from a site near ancient Sparta.
swap.clue: Before becoming emperor, Constantine ruled this despotate that encompassed much of the Peloponnese peninsula whose capital was Mystras.
